findings.title: Tables without a usable key
findings.headline: 1 table
findings.verdict: 1 table in every user schema: review.no_pk_events.
findings.why: InnoDB keeps each table as a B-tree ordered by the primary key, and every secondary index stores the primary key to reach the row. Without a primary key it uses the first unique key on NOT NULL columns (whole columns, not a prefix, a virtual generated column). Without one it adds a hidden 6-byte row ID. With row-based replication (the default) each UPDATE or DELETE reaches the replica as the changed rows, and the replica has to find each one. With a primary key or a unique key on NOT NULL columns that is one index lookup per row. Without one, MySQL 5.7 with its default slave_rows_search_algorithms (INDEX_SCAN,TABLE_SCAN) looks each row up through another index if there is one, or else reads the table from the start for every changed row: deleting 10,000 rows can mean 10,000 table scans, and the replica falls behind.
findings.rule: problem: no PRIMARY KEY and no UNIQUE key on NOT NULL columns
findings.caveat: Adding a primary key rebuilds the table: it takes time and free disk space for a new copy of the table, and replicas run the same ALTER after it finishes here, so they lag while they rebuild. ALGORITHM=INPLACE, LOCK=NONE makes the server refuse instead of blocking writes when it cannot do it online, for example with a FULLTEXT or SPATIAL index, or when columns must become NOT NULL outside strict SQL mode. Adding an AUTO_INCREMENT column always blocks writes (LOCK=SHARED). The ALTER waits for transactions that use the table, and queries on it queue behind that wait. Try it on a copy or a replica first.

action.text: Add a primary key; Tables has the checks to run first and the statement for each table.

This MySQL does not report the checkpoint age as a status counter (the Innodb_redo_log_current_lsn and Innodb_redo_log_checkpoint_lsn counters are MySQL 8.0.30 and later), so only the write rate is judged here; the LOG section of SHOW ENGINE INNODB STATUS shows Log sequence number and Last checkpoint at. A larger redo log smooths that out but makes crash recovery longer. This server does not report Innodb_redo_log_current_lsn (MySQL before 8.0.30), so the rate uses Innodb_os_log_written, the bytes written to the redo files, which re-counts the last partly filled block on each write and so runs high. findings.verdict: The buffer pool is full (1,024 free pages, at or below the page cleaner's target of 1,024) and InnoDB read almost nothing from disk: 0 pages per second (0 B/s). The data this workload uses fits in memory.
findings.why: InnoDB keeps a small free list: while the server is busy, its page cleaner evicts the least recently used pages until each buffer pool instance has innodb_lru_scan_depth free pages, and an idle full pool can show 0 free pages (1,024 x 1 = 1,024 pages here). So "full" means free pages at or below that target, not zero. Once it is full, every page read from disk evicts another one. Bytes read from disk are the pages read from disk times innodb_page_size (16.0 KiB); MySQL adds Innodb_buffer_pool_read_ahead, because Innodb_buffer_pool_reads leaves out linear read-ahead. Innodb_data_read counts the bytes InnoDB read from its data files: it is lower for ROW_FORMAT=COMPRESSED tables, which read the smaller compressed page, and on MySQL it also counts redo log reads, but only during startup.
findings.rule: full when free pages are at or below innodb_lru_scan_depth x buffer pool instances (the free list InnoDB's page cleaner keeps). Full: ok below 10 pages read from disk per second, watch at 10 or more, problem when the hit ratio is also below 95%. Not full: no threshold

findings.title: Tables clustered on a unique key, not a primary key
findings.headline: 0 tables
findings.verdict: None in every user schema.
findings.why: InnoDB keeps each table as a B-tree ordered by the primary key, and every secondary index stores the primary key to reach the row. Without a primary key it uses the first unique key on NOT NULL columns (whole columns, not a prefix, a virtual generated column). Without one it adds a hidden 6-byte row ID. With row-based replication (the default) each UPDATE or DELETE reaches the replica as the changed rows, and the replica has to find each one. With a primary key or a unique key on NOT NULL columns that is one index lookup per row. Without one, MySQL 5.7 with its default slave_rows_search_algorithms (INDEX_SCAN,TABLE_SCAN) looks each row up through another index if there is one, or else reads the table from the start for every changed row: deleting 10,000 rows can mean 10,000 table scans, and the replica falls behind.
findings.rule: watch: no PRIMARY KEY, but a UNIQUE key on NOT NULL columns stands in for it
